newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kohl urges Japan, Germany to stand up for peace.
newsitem.headline: Kohl urges Japan, Germany to stand up for peace.

text.p: Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl wound up a trip to Japan on Saturday saying the two countries had to stand up for world peace and human rights.
Kohl said Germany and Japan had the obligation as rich nations to help those who could not help themselves and to fight for free trade and protection of the environment.
"Our recent past obliges us to stand up for peace, freedom, human rights and democracy," Kohl said after receiving an honorary doctorate at Keio University.
Germany and Japan were both aggressors in World War Two.
Kohl arrived in Japan on Thursday on the last leg of an Asian tour that also included the Philippines and Indonesia to promote German business interests in the fast-growing area.
During a meeting with Japanese business leaders, Kohl stressed the importance of integrating China into the international community despite human rights concerns.
"It is better to tackle human rights issues in coordination with economics, though the United States tells us not to see only its economy," Kyodo news agency quoted Kohl as saying.

Kohl, who has come under attack at home for playing down human rights in Indonesia, tried to arrange a meeting with East Timorese Nobel Prize laureate Bishop Carlos Belo during his stay but Belo turned down his invitation.
Kohl, who on Thursday broke Konrad Adenauer's record to become Germany's longest-serving chancellor this century, met Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Tokyo on Friday.
They agreed to hold summits every year, with their next meeting scheduled for June in Denver where the G-7 meeting of industrialised nations will take place.

During his three-day visit, he also met Emperor Akihito and visited the Tokyo Stock Exchange, where shares of Deutsche Telekom AG will be listed later this month in the country's largest privatisation project.

Asked about the U.N. Security Council, where both Germany and Japan aspire to permanent membership, Kohl only said it was necessary to reform the United Nations to adjust its structure for the next century.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said in Germany on Friday that giving Germany a permanent seat on the Security Council would bring the world body up to date with economic and political reality.
On his way back to Bonn, Kohl planned a stop in Moscow to meet Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
